title: Mexico in the Work of a Modest Revolutionary
author: Jaime Ortega
content:
_This article by[Jaime
Ortega](https://www.jornada.com.mx/autores/Jaime%20Ortega) originally appeared
in the [November 5, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/11/05/opinion/mexico-en-la-
obra-de-un-modesto-revolucionario), Mexico's premier left wing daily
newspaper._

The most besieged figure in these days of anti-Cuban offensive is Raúl Castro,
whose middle name seems to be performative of his attitude toward the island’s
revolutionary process: Modesto. This mark of identity was recognized by his
biographer and friend, the Russian-Soviet Nikolai Leónov. In left-wing
political circles his discursive practice is less referenced, and only in
recent times, with the appearance of the **nine volumes of his _Selected
Works_** (in collaboration with the People’s Republic of China), can we delve
into a more complete panorama of his political vision. Important antecedents
were the two volumes titled _Selection of Speeches and Articles_ , which
collect public appearances between 1976 and 1986, and the two volumes titled
_Revolution: The Most Beautiful Work_ , with addresses between 2006 and 2018.
In Mexico some of his speeches were published in the _Revista de la
Universidad_ in 1959, and in the 1970s in _Cuadernos Políticos_ and _Historia
y Sociedad_.

As historians from the Office of Historical Affairs, José Luis Aneiros and
Dayli Sánchez, pointed out during the Havana International Book Fair last
August, these volumes allow the discovery of a figure whose linguistic
richness goes hand in hand with political passion. It is true that, unlike his
brother Fidel, Raúl is a man much more devoted to the Cuban world. Although
his interventions on Latin America or global issues were not lacking, the
truth is that his political and intellectual craft is found, above all, in the
construction of Cuban institutions, especially the Defense apparatus.

The more than 5,000 pages give us access to documents that enrich the
documentary sources on the revolutionary process. The most emblematic case is
the first volume, which includes his diaries from the insurrectionary
struggle. A fascinating fragment of his diary is when he writes about how
books on the history of Cuba reached the Rebel Army, to be used for
ideological training, but also an algebra book requested by the “multifaceted”
Che Guevara, whom he acknowledges as the one who ordered all the bibliographic
material that arrived at the front.

Besides this, which will surely enrich the historiographic account of the
armed struggle, we can find some interesting facts regarding Mexico. For
example, it includes the interview conducted by Gerardo Unzueta, the veteran
and self-taught Mexican communist journalist. In 1959 Unzueta—at the time,
director of the PCM’s organ _La Voz de México_ —interviewed Che Guevara
(_Revista Memoria_ number 299) and also Raúl, whom he asked, in August of that
same year, for his characterization of the revolution. The general, surprised,
responds: “Honestly, since the war ended, no journalist had yet asked me such
a complex and extensive question in so few words.”

Another interesting fact that can be recognized in these pages is the presence
of General Cárdenas, whom Raúl refers to on numerous occasions as an
“illustrious son of Mexico,” and whom he credits with the “so selfless gesture
that brought him to our shores to fight as one more soldier of the
revolution.” At another moment he had called him “that glory, not of Mexico,
but of America.” Many years later, in September 1975, Raúl evokes in a speech,
in the presence of engineer Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, the brave acts and gestures
of his father, and gives the general’s grandson, “who has the honor and the
glory of bearing his name,” an “imperialist M-3 submachine gun,” telling him:
**“We could not give it to your grandfather, we give it to another Lázaro
Cárdenas.”** These pieces bring together elements for reflecting on the
dialogue, fragmentary but not interrupted, between the two deepest and most
far-reaching revolutions on the continent.

Finally, in the 1990s, in an interview published in _El Sol de México_
conducted by Mario Vázquez Raña, Raúl Modesto tells him about one of the most
dramatic moments in Cuba’s relationship with the Soviet Union: when, in the
early 1980s, at the moment of the neoconservative siege led by Reagan, the
Soviets let Raúl know that, **in the event of military aggression against
Cuba, they would not intervene**. Fidel and Raúl took on the responsibility of
containing that “so bitter” information, which was not disclosed by agreement
of the leadership bodies of the Communist Party. Incidentally, reading this
interview would cancel any evocation of Cuba as a Soviet “satellite,” an
ideological trope that continues to be repeated by “former ambassadors”
transmuted into academics in the classrooms of the Olympus of Ajusco (listen
to the September 16 edition of _Noticias Cabo Mil_).

The works of Raúl Modesto Castro represent a good pretext for broadening
historical knowledge of the politics of revolutionary Cuba. The Ediciones
Celia imprint has delivered valuable documentation to scholars, which
contributes to understanding the reasons and passions of one of the longest-
lived political leaders and, as of today, one of the most attacked by the
irrational imperial powers and their Latin American vassal hosts. This is,
perhaps, the most powerful reason to study him.

* * *
    
    
    Jaime Ortega  
    is a researcher at UAM and the author of _Ternura y tempestad: el centenario de Fidel y el horizonte de la liberación nacional_ (Rosa Luxemburg Foundation - Institute of Philosophy of Cuba).
